meta.description: Not Shakespeare. The line is Arrigo Boito's, sung by Fenton in Verdi's opera Falstaff (1893) — the English wording is a later paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When I saw you I fell in love, and you smiled because you knew'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Shakespeare. It's from Arrigo Boito's libretto for Verdi's Falstaff (1893), sung by Fenton. The popular English wording is an anonymous paraphrase.

answer.label: Not William Shakespeare — actually Arrigo Boito
answer.sourceLine: The line is not Shakespeare’s — it is spoken by young Fenton in Verdi’s 1893 opera Falstaff, from a libretto by Arrigo Boito: “Come ti vidi m’innamorai, e tu sorridi perché lo sai.” Boito adapted Shakespeare’s The Merry Wives of Windsor and Henry IV, but this couplet is his own invention; the popular English wording is a later, anonymous rendering of his Italian. As Quote Investigator ↗ puts it, “Boito should be credited.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Libretto by Arrigo Boito; music by Giuseppe Verdi
Act II, Part 2 — sung by Fenton to Nannetta
Popular English wording is an anonymous modern rendering; cf. William Weaver (1977)

source.excerpt:
Come ti vidi
M’innamorai,
E tu sorridi
Perché lo sai.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ searched Shakespeare’s complete works, found nothing, and traced the line to Fenton in Boito’s libretto for Verdi’s Falstaff.
The original Italian — “Come ti vidi m’innamorai, e tu sorridi perché lo sai” — is documented for Arrigo Boito ↗, librettist of Otello and Falstaff.
Because Falstaff is built from The Merry Wives of Windsor and Henry IV, the line is constantly re-tagged “William Shakespeare” — but it appears in none of his plays.
source.excerptNote: Fenton’s lines in Boito’s Italian libretto. William Weaver’s 1977 English translation renders them “When I saw you / I fell in love, / And you smile / Because you know it” — the widely shared “you smiled because you knew” is a smoother, unattributed paraphrase of that idea.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: origin traced to Boito's Falstaff libretto

source.rightsNote: Boito’s Italian libretto premiered in 1893 and is long in the public domain. But the exact English wording people share is not a documented published translation — it is an anonymous paraphrase that differs from the standard William Weaver translation (1977, itself still in copyright). Because this precise English phrasing cannot be tied to a specific pre-1931 translation, its rights status is best treated as uncertain.

author.name: Arrigo Boito
author.heading: Who really wrote it
author.metaLine: 1842–1918 · Italian librettist, composer & poet — wrote the libretti for Verdi's Otello and Falstaff
author.bio: Arrigo Boito (1842–1918) was an Italian poet, composer and critic best remembered as the librettist who gave Giuseppe Verdi the texts for his two late Shakespearean masterpieces, Otello (1887) and Falstaff (1893). A learned man of letters, he reshaped Shakespeare’s comedy into taut Italian verse — and in the process wrote lyrical lines, like Fenton’s aside to Nannetta, that have no direct counterpart in the English plays.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most durable Shakespeare misattributions — feel-good, romantic, and pinned to the most bankable name in English literature. It is not his.

items.why: The line appears in none of Shakespeare’s plays or sonnets; a full-text search of his works turns up nothing, per Quote Investigator ↗. It is credited to him only because Verdi’s Falstaff is drawn from his comedies.
Some collections (e.g. the 2008 book 101 Ways to Say Thank You) specifically cite Romeo and Juliet, as noted by Quote Investigator ↗. The couplet is not in that play either.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Fenton’s in Arrigo Boito’s libretto for Verdi’s Falstaff (1893) — “Come ti vidi m’innamorai, e tu sorridi perché lo sai” — and Quote Investigator ↗ concludes “Boito should be credited.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line has the ring of Shakespeare because it lives inside his world — but at one remove. When Verdi and Boito adapted The Merry Wives of Windsor and Henry IV into the opera Falstaff, Boito wrote fresh Italian verse for the young lovers Fenton and Nannetta. This couplet is his, not the Bard’s.

Stripped of the opera and passed hand to hand online in English, it lost its author twice over: first Boito’s name, then the translator’s, until only “William Shakespeare” remained on the poster, mug, or wedding invitation.
context.pull: The words are sung, not spoken — by Boito’s pen, to Verdi’s music.
